  "core_problem": "Test-time compute scaling (TTS) dramatically improves LLM reasoning on scalar-answer tasks, but IE outputs are structured objects (entity sets, relation graphs, event frames) with no clear verification function. We ask: when and why does sampling multiple schema-constrained extractions and aggregating via structural consistency improve IE — and when does it fail?",
  "opportunity": "TTS is the dominant paradigm for boosting LLM reasoning (DeepSeek-R1, o1), yet its application to structured prediction remains unexplored. Two critical findings frame this gap: (1) PMC12888769 shows weak consistency-accuracy correlation for IE using surface-level Fleiss' Kappa on zero-shot models (Spearman 0.20–0.28 across GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, Kimi, Qwen3), questioning whether consistency-based selection can work at all — but the authors explicitly note that fine-tuned models 'could exhibit different consistency–accuracy dynamics'; (2) arXiv 2509.06861 argues TTS cannot help knowledge-intensive tasks because sampling cannot inject new information. We hypothesize that both findings admit an important exception: for fine-tuned IE models, a significant fraction of errors are uncertainty-based (boundary detection, type ambiguity, structural composition) rather than knowledge-gap errors — and structural consistency (not surface string matching) can identify correct extractions in this regime. Critically, we validate this hypothesis with a small-scale pilot before committing full compute, addressing the unvalidated assumption concern directly. XGrammar (MLSys 2025) makes constrained sampling near-free (<40μs/token via vLLM's default backend), and mature UIE models (ProUIE, GoLLIE) provide strong base samplers. Concurrent work on multi-model NER ensembles (EL4NER, ACL 2025 submission) aggregates across different models via span-level similarity for ICL retrieval, but no work samples from a single fine-tuned model and aggregates via structural consistency over the outputs — our approach isolates TTS contribution from model diversity, directly testing whether self-consistency scaling works for structured IE.",
  "landscape": "Test-time scaling is extensively studied for math/code (Forest-of-Thought, ICML 2025; Parallel TTS, Oct 2025; 30B+ token study, Dec 2024) but targets scalar-answer tasks exclusively. Self-consistency voting (Wang et al., ICLR 2023) and its successors — Reasoning-Aware Self-Consistency (NAACL 2025), inverse-entropy weighted voting (arXiv Nov 2025), Radial Consensus Score (arXiv April 2026), confidence-informed SC (arXiv Feb 2025), Ranked Voting SC (ACL 2025 Findings) — all aggregate scalar, embedding-space, or ranked-list answers. No work defines structural self-consistency for IE outputs. In IE, ProUIE (April 2026) achieves SOTA via GRPO with stepwise fine-grained rewards on Qwen3-4B (ACE05-NER: 86.15 F1, ACE05-Arg: 52.58 F1, avg NER: 79.44, avg RE: 71.17), and MR-UIE (Sept 2025) applies multi-perspective reasoning with RL — but both are training-time methods that generate single-pass outputs at inference. Two lines of post-hoc correction work are relevant but distinct: (a) VerifiNER (ACL 2024) uses knowledge-grounded verification via external KB retrieval as post-hoc NER correction, achieving +20% average precision on GENIA/BC5CDR — this represents a KB-dependent paradigm complementary to our KB-free self-consistency approach; (b) EL4NER (arXiv 2505.23038) ensembles multiple small LLMs for NER using span-level sentence similarity for ICL demo retrieval and a self-validation mechanism — but aggregates across different models (multi-model ensemble) rather than sampling from one model (single-model self-consistency), and targets zero-shot ICL settings rather than fine-tuned extraction. SaM (ACL 2025) dynamically selects and merges domain-specific NER expert models at inference, again a multi-model approach. Critically, PMC12888769 (2026) measured consistency-accuracy correlation for IE using Fleiss' Kappa on zero-shot hard-prompted models for document-level RE, finding weak Spearman correlations (0.20–0.28). However, their methodology differs fundamentally from ours in two ways: (1) they used surface string matching on un-fine-tuned models, while we propose structural consistency (soft span overlap, graph consensus, frame alignment) on task-specific fine-tuned models, and (2) they acknowledged this limitation, noting fine-tuned approaches 'could exhibit different consistency–accuracy dynamics.' The 'Two Failures of Self-Consistency' (Chen et al., 2023) demonstrates poor compositional consistency in multi-step reasoning — IE has compositional structure (entity → relation → event) that may exhibit similar failures, which we explicitly test. No concurrent work applies test-time sampling with structural aggregation from a single fine-tuned model to IE — confirmed via arXiv and OpenReview searches through May 2026.",
  "approach": "We propose Structural Self-Consistency Scaling (S2CS) as both a method and an empirical framework for understanding when TTS helps structured IE. The research is structured in two phases: a pilot validation (Phase 0) that tests the core assumption before committing full compute, followed by the full experimental study (Phase 1).\n\n**Phase 0: Pilot Validation (~5h H100, Days 1–2)**\nBefore committing to the full study, we run a targeted pilot to validate the core premise that structural consistency correlates better with extraction accuracy than surface-level metrics on fine-tuned models. Using 200 instances from ACE05 NER, we sample N=8 extractions at T=0.9 from the fine-tuned Qwen3-8B model and compute: (a) Fleiss' Kappa on surface string matches (replicating PMC12888769's methodology), (b) our soft Jaccard span-level structural consistency score, and (c) Spearman correlation of each metric with per-instance F1 against gold annotations. If structural consistency yields significantly stronger correlation than Fleiss' Kappa (target: Spearman ≥0.40 vs. their 0.20–0.28), we proceed to the full study. If both metrics show weak correlation (≤0.30), we diagnose why and either revise the aggregation design or pivot the paper to a negative/analytical result characterizing why TTS fundamentally cannot help structured IE — a valuable finding in itself that takes only ~20h additional compute to properly characterize.\n\n**Base Models**: We use Qwen3-8B fine-tuned on UIE instruction data (JSON output format, trained with LLaMA Factory following ProUIE's pipeline) as our primary model, and GoLLIE-7B (pre-trained, publicly available) as a cross-architecture generalization check. Using Qwen3-8B (not 32B) ensures fair comparison: the primary baseline is single-pass Qwen3-8B with greedy decoding from the same model, isolating TTS contribution from model scale.\n\n**Sampling**: For each input, we sample N ∈ {4, 8, 16, 32} schema-constrained extractions via XGrammar-backed structured generation in vLLM with temperature T ∈ {0.7, 1.0} (bracketing the effective range; pilot validates T=0.9 is interpolatable), enforcing valid JSON output at near-zero overhead.\n\n**Structural Consistency Aggregation**: Three functions tailored to IE subtask structure: (1) span-level entity voting via soft Jaccard similarity over character offsets with type-aware grouping (threshold τ_span), (2) relation-level graph consensus via edge majority voting after entity coreference alignment using mention overlap (threshold τ_coref), (3) event-level frame aggregation via trigger-anchored slot matching with role-wise majority voting (threshold τ_trigger for trigger matching). A composite structural agreement score ranks candidates or constructs a merged consensus output.\n\n**Aggregation Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis**: Each aggregation function depends on a threshold parameter. We report sensitivity sweeps: τ_span ∈ {0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.8}, τ_coref ∈ {0.3, 0.5, 0.7}, τ_trigger ∈ {0.5, 0.7, 0.9}. We report F1 variance across threshold settings per dataset to assess reproducibility and fragility of the contribution.\n\n**Ablation Framework**: We report four baselines to contextualize aggregation gains: (a) single-pass greedy (same model, no TTS), (b) random-of-N (random selection from N samples — lower bound), (c) naive majority voting (surface string matching, no structural alignment — directly replicating the methodology of PMC12888769 on our fine-tuned models), (d) oracle best-of-N (select sample with highest F1 against gold — upper bound). The gap between oracle and single-pass bounds the achievable gain; the gap between S2CS and naive-majority isolates the value of structural aggregation functions. Additionally, we include VerifiNER as a paradigm comparison on NER subtasks: both are post-hoc correction methods, but VerifiNER relies on external KB retrieval while S2CS uses only self-consistency — this comparison reveals whether KB-grounded verification or self-consistency is more effective for different error types.\n\n**Error Taxonomy Analysis** (key analytical contribution): We categorize model errors into: (i) uncertainty errors — correct extraction appears in at least one of N samples but not deterministically (TTS can help via consistency filtering), (ii) knowledge-gap errors — correct extraction never appears in any sample regardless of N (TTS fundamentally cannot help), (iii) systematic errors — model consistently produces the same wrong output (TTS cannot help). We report the fraction of each error type per dataset and subtask, directly addressing the knowledge-intensive limitation critique from arXiv 2509.06861. This taxonomy determines the theoretical ceiling for TTS gains in IE.\n\n**Compositional Consistency Analysis**: Following the 'Two Failures' work, we measure consistency at atomic (entity) vs. compositional (relation, event frame) granularity to test whether IE's multi-step structure degrades self-consistency for complex extractions.\n\n**Evaluation**: 5 datasets covering all IE subtasks — ACE05 (NER+RE+EE, the canonical multi-task IE benchmark), Few-NERD (fine-grained NER with 66 entity types, providing more headroom than saturated CoNLL03), SciERC (NER+RE, scientific domain), TACREV (sentence-level RE, revised annotations addressing known TACRED issues), WikiEvents (document-level event argument extraction). We report F1 with bootstrap significance tests (p<0.05), scaling curves (F1 vs. N and vs. total compute), cost-accuracy Pareto frontiers, and error taxonomy distributions.",

## Reviewer feedback (round 3)
Issues: ["MODERATE — NO CONFIDENCE-GATED SELECTIVE APPLICATION: Applying TTS uniformly to all instances wastes compute on easy examples where single-pass already extracts correctly. Active concurrent work on adaptive TTS (ReASC, arXiv 2601.02970; CGES, arXiv 2511.02603; 'Learning When to Sample', arXiv 2603.08999; Sonata/CoRefine) shows that confidence-gated early stopping can reduce sampling budget by 60-80% with negligible accuracy loss. S2CS should leverage structural consistency scores to gate TTS application: if N=4 samples already show high agreement, skip further sampling. This would dramatically improve the cost-accuracy Pareto frontier and make the method practically deployable, directly addressing the concern that 16-32x compute for 1-3 F1 is not cost-effective.", "MODERATE — AGGREGATION FUNCTIONS ARE THRESHOLD-BASED HEURISTICS: The three structural aggregation functions each depend on manually-set thresholds (τ_span, τ_coref, τ_trigger) with sensitivity sweeps over a small grid. While the sensitivity analysis is appreciated, a purely threshold-based approach is fragile and hard to transfer across datasets/domains. Consider adding a lightweight learned aggregation scorer (e.g., a small MLP trained on pilot data features — span overlap distribution, type agreement entropy, structural graph features — to predict extraction quality). This would provide a principled alternative to hand-crafted heuristics and add genuine technical novelty beyond task-specific engineering.", "MINOR — MISSING CITATION: STED (arXiv 2512.23712, NeurIPS 2025 Workshop): 'STED and Consistency Scoring: A Framework for Evaluating LLM Structured Output Reliability' introduces Semantic Tree Edit Distance for measuring consistency of structured JSON outputs across repeated LLM generations. While it is an evaluation framework rather than an extraction improvement method, it directly addresses structural consistency measurement for structured LLM outputs — the same conceptual space as S2CS. The paper should cite STED and discuss how its consistency scoring approach relates to the proposed structural agreement score.", "MINOR — HEADROOM CEILING RISK ON SATURATED SUBTASKS: ProUIE achieves 86.15 F1 on ACE05 NER with Qwen3-4B. A fine-tuned Qwen3-8B single-pass may reach 87-88 F1, leaving <2 F1 headroom for oracle best-of-N improvement. If the oracle ceiling is low, S2CS gains will be negligible on this subtask. The paper should report oracle best-of-N gaps per dataset/subtask early (Phase 0 or early Phase 1) and concentrate analysis on subtasks with meaningful headroom (event argument extraction at ~52 F1 has much more room). Consider adding a headroom-aware analysis section that correlates TTS gains with base performance level.", "MINOR — ADAPTIVE TTS LITERATURE NOT ENGAGED: The proposal applies a fixed N across all instances. A rapidly growing literature on adaptive test-time compute allocation (Sonata for thinking budget allocation, CoRefine for confidence-guided refinement, CGES for Bayesian early stopping, ReASC for reliability-aware sampling) is directly relevant. The paper should at minimum discuss these works and ideally implement adaptive N as an efficiency-oriented variant of S2CS."]
Feedback: The Round 3 revision is substantially improved — all Round 1 and Round 2 issues have been addressed. The pilot-gated design, error taxonomy, rigorous ablation framework, and engagement with counter-evidence (PMC12888769, arXiv 2509.06861, 'Two Failures') are all strong. The proposal is close to passing but needs two targeted improvements to reach the novelty and impact thresholds:

1. **Add confidence-gated selective TTS (biggest impact on both novelty and practical value)**: Don't apply N=32 samples uniformly. Use structural consistency at N=4 as a confidence signal: if early samples already agree strongly, accept the result and skip further sampling. Only invest N=16-32 on instances with low early consistency. This connects to the active adaptive TTS literature (ReASC, CGES, 'Learning When to Sample') but applies it to structured prediction for the first time — a genuine novelty contribution. It also makes the method practically deployable by reducing average compute from 32x to perhaps 6-8x while preserving most gains, dramatically improving the cost-accuracy Pareto frontier.

2. **Add a learned aggregation variant**: Beyond the three hand-crafted threshold-based functions, train a lightweight scoring model on Phase 0 pilot data to predict extraction quality from structural features (span overlap distribution, type agreement entropy, consistency pattern across N samples). This provides a principled alternative to manual threshold tuning, improves cross-dataset transfer, and adds genuine technical depth. The comparison between hand-crafted vs. learned aggregation would itself be an interesting finding.

3. **Cite STED (arXiv 2512.23712)** and discuss how its structured output consistency evaluation framework relates to your structural agreement score.

4. **Report headroom gaps early**: Include oracle best-of-N F1 gaps per dataset/subtask in Phase 0 or early Phase 1, and adjust analysis emphasis toward subtasks with meaningful headroom (EAE > RE > NER likely).

These additions would push novelty from 3.5→4.0 and impact from 3.5→4.0, bringing the average to the pass threshold. The experimental design is already strong enough to support these additions within the compute budget.

- Think in two phases: FIRST reconsider the problem framing (core_problem / opportunity / landscape) if the reviewer flagged issues there, THEN revise the method (approach / resource_estimate / key_references). Do not jump straight to fixing the method if the underlying problem framing needs correction.
- Address each issue specifically.

## 深度调研要求（每一轮修订都必须执行）

不要简单地'打补丁'——每一轮修订都是重新审视和深化这个 idea 的机会。

1. **深度搜索**：针对 reviewer 指出的每个问题，建议用 2-3 种不同的搜索查询调研。
   - 搜索最新的相关论文（arXiv, conference proceedings）
   - 搜索 benchmark/leaderboard 确认当前 SOTA
   - 搜索可能遗漏的相关工作和 concurrent work

2. **深度阅读**：用 WebFetch 实际阅读找到的关键论文的 abstract 和方法部分，
   不要只依赖搜索摘要。形成你自己对领域现状的独立判断。

3. **深度思考**：在修订之前，先独立思考以下问题：
   - 这个 idea 的核心假设是否仍然成立？
   - reviewer 的批评是否揭示了更深层的问题？
   - 有没有更好的 framing 或 approach 来解决同一个核心问题？
   - 修订后的 idea 相比上一版有什么本质性的改进？

4. **避免表面修订**：如果你发现自己只是在换措辞或补充细节而没有实质改进，
   考虑是否需要 major revision 或 pivot。反复的 minor fix 不会拯救一个根基有问题的 idea。

## 针对 Review 意见的定向搜索

对 reviewer 指出的每个问题，执行以下搜索流程：

1. **如果 reviewer 说'已有类似工作'**：
   - 搜索 reviewer 提到的论文，用 WebFetch 实际阅读
   - 搜索该论文的 cited-by，找到后续跟进工作
   - 明确你的 idea 与这些工作的差异化点——如果差异化不够，必须 pivot

2. **如果 reviewer 说'SOTA 过时'**：
   - 用 Papers With Code 查看当前排行榜
   - 搜索过去 6 个月的最新方法
   - 更新你的 landscape 和 baseline

3. **如果 reviewer 说'可行性有问题'**：
   - 搜索类似规模实验的实际成本和时间线
   - 搜索 GitHub 上是否有可复用的实现
   - 搜索相关数据集/模型的可获取性

4. **如果 reviewer 说'novelty 不足'**：
   - 对核心方法尽量做 3-5 种不同关键词组合的搜索
   - 搜索相邻领域是否有类似思路
   - 如果确实 novelty 不足，考虑 major revision 或 pivot

- Use WebSearch to find updated information if the reviewer flagged outdated claims.
- You have full freedom in how much to change:
  - Minor fix: if only specific details are wrong, correct them and keep everything else.
  - Major revision: if the approach is fundamentally flawed but the core problem is valid, you may redesign the approach entirely.
  - Pivot: if the reviewer's feedback reveals that the core problem itself is invalid (e.g., the gap no longer exists), you may propose a RELATED but substantially different idea that builds on the same research area. This is preferred over forcing a doomed idea to pass review.
- The output replaces the original idea (same tracking ID). Whether you make a small tweak or a full pivot, output a COMPLETE JSON object with ALL fields filled.
- In the output JSON, include a "change_type" field with one of: "minor", "major", or "pivot" to indicate the scope of your changes.
- Output the revised idea as a COMPLETE JSON object (same schema as original, plus "change_type").

## Overview

ReASC (Reliability-Aware Adaptive Self-Consistency) addresses the limitation of adaptive sampling by reframing it from response counting to evidence sufficiency, leveraging response-level confidence for principled information aggregation.

## Key Problem

Self-Consistency improves reasoning reliability through multi-sample aggregation, but incurs substantial inference cost. Adaptive self-consistency methods mitigate this issue by adjusting the sampling budget; however, they rely on count-based stopping rules that treat all responses equally, often leading to unnecessary sampling.

## How ReASC Works

ReASC operates in two stages: a single-sample decision stage that resolves instances confidently answerable from a single response, and a reliability-aware accumulation stage that aggregates responses by jointly leveraging their frequency and confidence.

## Performance Results

ReASC reduces inference cost by up to 70% relative to self-consistency while preserving accuracy on GSM8K using Gemma-3-4B-it. Across five models and four datasets, ReASC consistently achieves the best accuracy-cost trade-off compared to existing baselines.

The paper was authored by researchers from Seoul National University and was submitted to arXiv on January 6, 2026.

## "Learning When to Sample: Confidence-Aware Self-Consistency for Efficient LLM Chain-of-Thought Reasoning"

**arXiv ID:** 2603.08999

**Key Details:**

Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong reasoning performance through chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, yet often generate unnecessarily long reasoning paths that incur high inference cost. Recent self-consistency-based approaches further improve accuracy but require sampling and aggregating multiple reasoning trajectories, leading to substantial additional computational overhead.

**Main Contribution:**

The paper introduces a confidence-aware decision framework that analyzes a single completed reasoning trajectory to adaptively select between single-path and multi-path reasoning. Instead of relying on multi-path sampling, the method dynamically decides whether to continue or terminate generation based on sentence-level numeric and linguistic features that capture confidence, uncertainty, and temporal reasoning dynamics.

**Results:**

The framework is trained using sentence-level numeric and linguistic features extracted from intermediate reasoning states in the MedQA dataset and generalizes effectively to MathQA, MedMCQA, and MMLU without additional fine-tuning. Experimental results show that the proposed method maintains accuracy comparable to multi-path baselines while using up to 80% fewer tokens.

The paper introduces STED (Semantic Tree Edit Distance), a novel similarity metric that balances semantic flexibility with structural strictness when comparing JSON outputs, combined with a consistency scoring framework that aggregates multiple STED measurements across repeated generations to quantify reliability.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for structured data generation, yet output consistency remains critical for production applications, and the paper introduces a comprehensive framework for evaluating and improving consistency in LLM-generated structured outputs.

## Sonata: Adaptive Thinking Budget Allocation

Sonata (Self-Consistency-Guided Adapter for Thinking Allocation) is a lightweight approach that adaptively allocates thinking budgets to optimize the performance-efficiency tradeoff.

### How It Works

Conventional approaches allocate all queries the same fixed thinking budget (e.g. 4k tokens each) during thinking, regardless of query complexity, resulting in suboptimal token allocation. Sonata addresses this by using self-consistency, the agreement among multiple reasoning paths, as a proxy for thinking necessity.

The adapter learns to predict self-consistency from last-layer hidden states. For each calibration query, the LLM generates multiple responses and self-consistency is computed as the accuracy among all sampled answers. The adapter is trained to map the last hidden states to these self-consistency scores.

### Performance and Efficiency

Extensive experiments on multiple models (Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B, GPT-OSS-120B, Qwen3-235B-A22B) and benchmarks (AIME25, GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA, LiveCodeBench) demonstrate that Sonata achieves 20% to 60% reduction in thinking tokens while maintaining the same accuracy, or up to 2% improvement in accuracy with the same token cost.

### Technical Benefits

The adapter is general, transferable across diverse tasks once trained, and introduces <1‰ computational overhead during inference. Additionally, Sonata is compatible with existing CoT compression methods, enabling further efficiency gains when managing thinking budgets across queries.

## CoRefine: Confidence-Guided Self-Refinement for Adaptive Test-Time Compute

CoRefine is a confidence-guided self-refinement method that achieves competitive accuracy using a fraction of the tokens via a lightweight 211k-parameter Conv1D controller atop a frozen LLM.

### Key Features and Mechanism

The controller consumes full-trace confidence features of the LLM decoded reasoning chain and decides: HALT (accept current answer), RETHINK (verify reasoning), or ALTERNATIVE (explore new approach).

### Performance and Efficiency

CoRefine saves up to 63% over parallel baselines in wall-clock time versus accuracy, showing that token savings translate to actual latency reduction. CoRefine's token reduction yields 63% wall-clock speedup over Majority@20, with an average of 2.7 iterations incurring minimal sequential overhead.

### Evaluation

CoRefine was evaluated across diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks (AIME 2024/2025, HMMT 2025, BRUMO25) and multiple open-source models (DeepSeek-8B, Qwen3-32B).

### CoRefine Tree Variant

For problems requiring both exploration and refinement, CoRefine Tree combines parallel sampling with sequential refinement in a tree structure. It operates in three phases: (1) Warmup: Sample K initial traces in parallel (e.g., K = 4), extracting confidence and answers from each. (2) Branching Refinement: Each trace marked for refinement spawns multiple children (branch factor B, default B = 2), creating a tree where promising directions are explored in parallel.

# STED and Consistency Scoring Framework Summary

## Abstract
The research introduces a comprehensive evaluation framework for LLM-generated structured data. As stated: "Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for structured data generation, yet output consistency remains critical for production applications."

## Core Method Details

The framework combines two main components:

1. **STED (Semantic Tree Edit Distance)**: A novel similarity metric that balances semantic flexibility with structural strictness when comparing JSON outputs

2. **Consistency Scoring Framework**: Aggregates multiple STED measurements across repeated generations to quantify reliability

## How STED Measures Consistency

The metric handles the structural-semantic tradeoff by:
- Achieving "0.86-0.90 similarity for semantic equivalents" (semantically identical outputs scored highly)
- Returning "0.0 for structural breaks" (fundamentally different JSON structures score zero)
- Outperforming existing metrics including TED, BERTScore, and DeepDiff

## Key Results

Testing across six LLMs revealed:
- Claude-3.7-Sonnet demonstrated "exceptional consistency, maintaining near-perfect structural reliability even at high temperatures"
- Models like Claude-3-Haiku and Nova-Pro showed "substantial degradation requiring careful tuning"

## Practical Applications

The framework enables model selection, prompt refinement, and diagnostic analysis to identify inconsistency sources in production systems.

# Reliability-Aware Adaptive Self-Consistency (ReASC) Summary

## Abstract
ReASC addresses inefficiencies in self-consistency by "reframing adaptive sampling from response counting to evidence sufficiency, leveraging response-level confidence for principled information aggregation."

## Two-Stage Approach

**Stage 1 - Single-Sample Decision:** The method identifies instances that can be confidently resolved using just one response, avoiding unnecessary additional sampling.

**Stage 2 - Reliability-Aware Accumulation:** Multiple responses are combined by jointly considering both their frequency and confidence scores, rather than treating all responses equally.

## Computational Efficiency
ReASC achieves superior accuracy-to-cost tradeoffs by using confidence signals to determine when sufficient evidence has been gathered. The paper demonstrates "up to 70% reduction in inference cost relative to self-consistency while preserving accuracy on GSM8K using Gemma-3-4B-it."

## Evaluation

**Models tested:** Five different models ranging from 3B to 27B parameters

**Datasets:** Four benchmark datasets (GSM8K explicitly mentioned)

**Results:** The approach "consistently achieves the best accuracy-cost trade-off compared to existing baselines, yielding improved inference efficiency across model scales."

The work was accepted to ACL 2026, with code publicly available on GitHub.

**description**: "We present Adaptive Structural Self-Consistency Scaling (AS2CS), the first systematic study of adaptive test-time compute scaling for structured information extraction. While self-consistency voting and its adaptive variants (ReASC, CGES, Sonata) have dramatically improved LLM reasoning efficiency on scalar-answer tasks — reducing sampling budgets by 60-80% via confidence-gated early stopping — IE outputs are structured objects (entity sets, relation graphs, event frames) where neither standard consistency measurement nor adaptive gating trivially applies. Recent evidence raises two challenges: weak consistency-accuracy correlations for IE using surface-level metrics on zero-shot models (PMC12888769), and the argument that TTS cannot help knowledge-intensive tasks (arXiv 2509.06861). We address both through a pilot-gated, headroom-aware research design. Our framework introduces three contributions beyond static structural aggregation: (1) Adaptive Structural Consistency Gating (ASCG), which uses structural agreement at N_min=4 samples as a confidence signal to decide whether to continue sampling — extending the adaptive TTS paradigm to structured prediction for the first time, where the key challenge is that the consistency signal itself requires structural alignment rather than simple answer agreement; (2) a Learned Aggregation Scorer (LAS), a lightweight MLP trained on pilot data to predict extraction quality from structural features (span overlap distribution, type agreement entropy, consistency trajectory), providing a principled alternative to hand-crafted threshold-based aggregation and enabling cross-dataset transfer analysis; (3) headroom-aware analysis that correlates TTS gains with base performance level to predict where TTS is worth applying. Our error taxonomy distinguishes uncertainty errors (TTS can help) from knowledge-gap errors (TTS cannot help), directly addressing the knowledge-intensive limitation. We connect our structural consistency measurement to STED's (arXiv 2512.23712) framework for evaluating structured JSON output reliability, but go beyond evaluation to leverage consistency for both aggregation and adaptive compute allocation. Using Qwen3-8B fine-tuned on UIE tasks and GoLLIE-7B, we sample schema-constrained extractions via XGrammar with near-zero overhead. Experiments across 5 benchmarks (ACE05, Few-NERD, SciERC, TACREV, WikiEvents) characterize not only compute-accuracy scaling curves and error-type distributions, but also cost-accuracy Pareto frontiers for adaptive vs. fixed sampling, the transferability of learned aggregation, and compositional consistency degradation — providing both a practical, compute-efficient method for improving IE via adaptive test-time scaling and a principled framework for understanding its limits."
